Sample text:
---
I keep thinking about used books. Not the stories printed in them — the other story, the one that accumulates around the edges.

A clean new book is perfect and a little lonely. A used book has been lived in. Someone has dog-eared the page where they fell asleep. Someone has underlined a sentence so hard the pen nearly tore through, as if to say *this, exactly this, I thought I was the only one who felt this.* In the margins there are arguments and agreements left by strangers: “yes!!” and “no — he’s lying” and, once in a while, in furious student handwriting next to a beautiful paragraph, “BORING.”

I love the accidental bookmarks most of all. Train tickets. Receipts for coffee and aspirin. A shopping list — milk, eggs, batteries, call Mum — abandoned halfway through chapter nine, which makes you wonder if they ever finished either the book or the errands. A dried flower pressed flat until it’s become almost translucent, more ghost than flower. Who picked it, and were they happy that day? You’ll never know. The book doesn’t tell you. It just keeps the evidence.

There’s something quietly radical about that kind of reading. We tend to imagine reading as a private act, one mind alone with another across time. But a used book turns it into a small, unplanned community. You are never actually the first person to be surprised by that plot twist. Someone else gasped there before you, maybe on a train in 1987, maybe in a hospital waiting room, maybe in bed while it rained. Their coffee ring is on the cover. Yours might be next.

Digital books are cleaner, lighter, searchable, objectively better in almost every practical way, and they will never smell faintly of someone else’s house. They won’t fall open naturally to the page that was read and reread until the spine gave up. They won’t betray that the previous owner read the first eighty pages enthusiastically, annotating everything, and then slowly stopped — fewer notes, then none — the literary equivalent of footprints trailing off in snow. Did they get busy? Get bored? Get their heart broken by chapter twelve? The silence is also part of the text.

I think that’s why I’m drawn to them: they’re proof that a life doesn’t have to be famous to leave a legible trace. Most of us won’t leave behind monuments. We’ll leave behind a highlighted sentence, a name written carefully inside a front cover, a note in the margin that makes some future stranger laugh in a quiet room. Small, unguarded moments of attention, preserved by accident.

Every book, it turns out, is two books. The one the author wrote, and the one its readers write back, slowly, in pencil, over decades.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A lyrical reflection turns the traces inside used books into a meditation on connection and ordinary lives.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate and observant, lingering over dog-eared pages, scribbled reactions, coffee rings, and abandoned bookmarks. Its pathos comes from the thought that these fragments preserve unfinished, uncelebrated lives without explaining them away. The reader is invited to treat a book not just as a private encounter with an author, but as a quiet meeting with strangers who read before them.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds used books as material evidence of past attention: annotations, receipts, flowers, fading marks, and eventual silence. It contrasts digital convenience with the physical book’s capacity to carry traces, and makes a gentle moral claim that an ordinary life can leave something legible without becoming famous.

## Evidence line
> The silence is also part of the text.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample’s distinctive, recurring focus on small material traces and their human meaning makes this a strong expression of that sensibility.
